blocks.text: A vector space is any collection of objects, arrows in a plane, columns of numbers, even functions, that can be added together and scaled by a number while always staying inside that same collection. This lesson names the rules that make vector arithmetic behave predictably everywhere it is used throughout this curriculum, from a 2D plane to a 1536 dimensional embedding space.

blocks.caption: The core ideas this lesson connects together

blocks.text: 1. What a Vector Space Is

A vector space is a set of objects, called vectors, together with two operations, addition and scalar multiplication, that always produce another object still inside that same set. Every vector and matrix operation covered earlier in this module, from the vector addition lesson through eigenvalues, has quietly been taking place inside a vector space the whole time.

blocks.alt: Every vector in the space stays inside its boundary
blocks.caption: Adding or scaling vectors never produces a result that escapes the space

blocks.text: Calling something a vector space is really a promise about how it behaves under these two operations, not a statement about what the objects themselves look like, which is why the concept stretches so comfortably from simple arrows to abstract objects like polynomials.

Everything from a single 2D arrow to an entire matrix, or an entire trained model weight tensor, can be legitimately treated as a single vector living inside some larger vector space, as long as it satisfies these same closure and structural rules.
2. The Rules a Vector Space Must Follow

Formally, a vector space must satisfy a short list of rules: addition is commutative and associative, there is a zero vector that changes nothing when added, every vector has an opposite that cancels it out to zero, and scalar multiplication distributes sensibly over both vector addition and scalar addition.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Rule","In plain language"],"rows":[["closure","adding or scaling vectors always lands back inside the space"],["zero vector exists","there is a do-nothing vector, like (0,0), that leaves any vector unchanged when added"],["additive inverse exists","every vector has an opposite that cancels it to zero when added"],["distributive scaling","scaling a sum equals the sum of the scaled parts"]]}

blocks.text: These rules rarely need to be checked explicitly in everyday work, but they are exactly what guarantees that formulas like vector addition and dot products behave the same predictable way no matter which vector space they are applied in.

Associative means grouping does not matter, (a plus b) plus c gives the same result as a plus (b plus c), and commutative means order does not matter, a plus b gives the same result as b plus a, both properties already relied upon implicitly throughout the vector addition lesson.

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: The zero vector in R3 is simply (0, 0, 0), adding it to any vector, such as (3, negative 1, 5), leaves that vector completely unchanged, exactly the identity role the number 0 plays in ordinary addition.

blocks.text: 3. Vector Spaces You Already Know

The ordinary 2D plane and 3D space, covered throughout this module, are the most familiar vector spaces, usually written R2 and R3. The same rules extend cleanly to R100, or R1536, an embedding space with 1536 dimensions, without needing any new machinery.

code.content:
import numpy as np
v1 = np.array([1, 2])   # a vector in R2
v2 = np.array([1, 2, 3])   # a vector in R3
v3 = np.random.rand(1536)   # a vector in R1536, same rules apply

blocks.text: The notation Rn, read R to the n, is standard shorthand throughout linear algebra and machine learning for the vector space of all vectors with n real number entries, worth recognizing on sight in papers and documentation.

Whether a space has 2 dimensions or 2000, every rule from section 2 continues to hold without modification, which is exactly why linear algebra techniques developed on small, easy to visualize examples generalize so reliably to the enormous dimensional spaces used in real machine learning systems.
4. Closure: Why It Matters

Closure, the requirement that adding or scaling vectors never leaves the space, is what makes it safe to chain vector operations together without checking after every single step whether the result is still valid. Without closure, a formula like weighted averaging several embeddings together could, in principle, produce something that is no longer a valid member of the same space.

code.content:
a = np.array([1, 2])
b = np.array([3, -1])
result = 0.5 * a + 0.5 * b   # a weighted average, still a vector in the same 2D space
print(result)

blocks.text: This becomes especially important in longer machine learning pipelines, where an embedding might be averaged, scaled, and added to another several times over before ever being used, closure guarantees every intermediate result along that chain remains a valid, well defined vector the whole way through.

Losing closure would mean a formula that worked correctly on some inputs could unpredictably break on others, exactly the kind of fragile, hard to debug behavior that a well defined vector space rules out from the start.
5. Subspaces Within a Vector Space

The basis and dimension lesson introduced subspaces, smaller vector spaces sitting entirely inside a larger one, such as a single line through the origin inside the 2D plane. A subspace must satisfy the exact same closure rules as the full space, adding or scaling any of its vectors must still land inside that smaller subspace, not just inside the larger space around it.

code.content:
# the line through the origin in direction (1, 1) is a valid subspace of R2
line_vec = np.array([1, 1])
scaled = 3 * line_vec        # still on the same line
combined = line_vec + 2 * line_vec   # still on the same line

blocks.text: Every subspace automatically contains the zero vector, since scaling any vector in the subspace by 0 must still land inside it, which is a quick, useful first check whenever testing whether a candidate set qualifies as a subspace.

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: The row space and column space introduced in the rank of matrix lesson are both concrete, working examples of subspaces, each one a smaller vector space sitting inside a larger space, exactly the pattern this section describes.

blocks.text: 6. Vector Spaces Beyond Arrows

The rules covered in section 2 apply to far more than arrows on a page. The set of all polynomials of degree 3 or less forms a vector space, since adding two such polynomials or scaling one by a number always produces another polynomial of degree 3 or less. Even the set of all 3 by 3 matrices forms a vector space, under ordinary matrix addition and scalar multiplication.

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: Adding the polynomials 2x squared plus 3 and negative x squared plus x gives x squared plus x plus 3, still a polynomial of degree 3 or less, exactly the closure property required of a valid vector space.

blocks.text: Recognizing that matrices themselves form a vector space explains why matrix addition and scalar multiplication of matrices, used throughout the matrix addition lesson, follow exactly the same familiar rules as ordinary vector arithmetic, nothing new needed to be learned for that lesson beyond relabeling the objects involved.

This generality is exactly why the same word, vector, gets reused across such different looking contexts throughout mathematics and machine learning, from arrows to functions to model weights, they are all instances of the same underlying formal structure.
7. Embedding Spaces Are Vector Spaces

Every embedding space used throughout modern AI systems, word embeddings, sentence embeddings, image embeddings, is a vector space in the exact formal sense covered in this lesson. That is precisely why averaging several embeddings together, or performing the famous king minus man plus woman analogy from the vector addition lesson, produces another valid point in that same embedding space rather than something meaningless.

items: Averaging multiple document embeddings to create a single representative embedding relies on closure, the average must remain a valid point in the same space.
Analogy arithmetic on word embeddings only makes sense because the embedding space satisfies the vector space rules covered in section 2.
Training a model to produce embeddings in a fixed dimensional space is, formally, choosing which vector space the model output must always land inside.

blocks.text: This formal guarantee is easy to take for granted precisely because it works so reliably in practice, but it is exactly why embedding arithmetic feels natural and predictable rather than fragile or undefined.

Two different embedding models rarely share the same vector space even if they happen to use the same dimension count, comparing embeddings from two different models directly, without a shared training process, generally produces meaningless results despite both being valid vectors in their own respective spaces.
8. What Is Not a Vector Space

Not every set of vectors qualifies as a vector space. The set of all vectors with strictly positive entries fails closure under scalar multiplication, since multiplying by negative 1 produces a vector with negative entries, outside the original set. Recognizing failures like this quickly avoids applying vector space assumptions where they silently do not hold.

code.content:
positive_only = np.array([2, 3])
scaled = -1 * positive_only
print(scaled)   # [-2, -3], no longer in the "all positive entries" set, so that set is not a vector space

blocks.text: A quick two-part test settles most cases quickly, add two members of the candidate set together and check the result is still a member, then scale a member by a negative number and check the same thing, failing either check rules the set out immediately.

Datasets constrained by real world requirements, like probabilities that must stay between 0 and 1, are a common example of sets that fail to form a vector space, since scaling or adding them can easily push a value outside that allowed range.
9. Linear Combinations and Span, Revisited

The basis and dimension lesson defined span as everywhere a set of vectors can reach through combined scaling and addition. A vector space can equivalently be described as the span of any one of its valid bases, every single vector in the space is reachable as some linear combination of basis vectors, and nothing outside the space is ever reachable that way.

code.content:
import numpy as np
e1 = np.array([1, 0])
e2 = np.array([0, 1])
# every vector in R2 is reachable as a*e1 + b*e2 for some real numbers a and b

blocks.text: This reframing means choosing a basis is really choosing a compact description of an entire vector space, every one of the infinitely many vectors it contains can be recovered from just a handful of basis vectors and the right combination of scalars.

This is the same reasoning that lets a machine learning model represent an enormous number of possible feature combinations using only a fixed, modest number of learned basis-like directions internally.
10. What Counts as a Scalar

The scalars used to scale vectors throughout this curriculum have always been ordinary real numbers, but the formal definition of a vector space allows the scalars to come from any mathematical field, a structure with its own addition and multiplication rules, most commonly the real numbers or the complex numbers. Everything covered in this module assumes real number scalars, which is the overwhelmingly common case in applied machine learning.

Complex number scalars appear in some signal processing and quantum computing contexts, but essentially never in the mainstream machine learning material this curriculum covers, real number scalars can safely be assumed throughout.

Being explicit about the scalar field matters mostly when reading advanced theoretical material, day to day applied work in this curriculum can safely treat scalar and real number as interchangeable terms.
11. Vector Spaces in Neural Network Layers

Every layer in a neural network transforms vectors from one vector space into vectors in another, an input layer might read from a 784 dimensional space, one entry per pixel, and a hidden layer might operate in a 256 dimensional space chosen by the model designer. Choosing a hidden layer size is, formally, choosing the dimension of the vector space that layer output must live in.

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: A transformer model with a hidden dimension of 768 defines every intermediate representation as a vector living inside R768, a specific, fixed vector space every layer, attention head, and residual connection is designed to respect consistently throughout the entire network.

blocks.text: Changing a hidden dimension from 768 to 1024 is, in this language, moving the layer output into a larger vector space entirely, with more independent directions available to represent learned features, directly echoing the dimension discussion from the basis and dimension lesson.

This is also why mismatched dimensions between two layers throw an immediate error rather than a subtle bug, the underlying frameworks are strictly enforcing that every vector passed between layers belongs to the exact vector space that layer expects.
12. A Worked Example
Confirm that the set of all 2D vectors whose two entries sum to 0, such as (3, negative 3) or (1, negative 1), forms a valid vector subspace of R2 by checking closure under addition and scaling.

code.content:
a = np.array([3, -3])
b = np.array([1, -1])
added = a + b
scaled = 2 * a
print(added, added.sum())    # sums still to 0
print(scaled, scaled.sum())  # sums still to 0

blocks.content: {"headers":["Check","Result"],"rows":[["sum of a + b","0"],["sum of 2 times a","0"],["valid subspace?","yes, closure holds for both operations"]]}

blocks.text: This particular subspace, all vectors whose entries sum to 0, is a 1 dimensional line through the origin in R2, exactly the kind of subspace the basis and dimension lesson described, describable entirely by a single basis vector like (1, negative 1).

Try one more check on your own, confirm the zero vector (0, 0) satisfies the sum-to-zero condition as well, completing the full set of checks needed to call this a genuine subspace rather than just an intuitively plausible one.
13. Common Mistakes

items: Assuming any collection of vector-shaped objects automatically forms a vector space without checking closure, as section 8 demonstrates, some intuitive sounding sets fail this test.
Forgetting that a subspace must contain the zero vector, a shifted line that does not pass through the origin fails to qualify as a subspace even though it looks similar to one that does.

Confusing the dimension of a vector space with the number of vectors currently being used to describe it, dimension is a fixed property of the space itself, covered fully in the basis and dimension lesson.

Assuming embedding arithmetic like averaging or analogy solving always produces a meaningful result just because it stays inside the vector space, closure guarantees validity as a vector, not that the result is semantically meaningful.

blocks.text: A related trap: assuming any subset that looks geometrically reasonable, like a circle or a curved surface, automatically qualifies as a subspace, most such shapes fail closure under both addition and scaling and are not vector spaces at all.
14. Practice: Check for Closure
Check whether the set of all 2D vectors whose entries are both whole numbers, such as (2, 3) or (negative 1, 4), is closed under scalar multiplication by any real number.

code.content:
whole_number_vec = np.array([2, 3])
scaled = 0.5 * whole_number_vec
print(scaled)   # [1. 1.5], no longer both whole numbers

items: Scaling by 0.5 produces a result with a non-whole entry, showing this set fails closure under scalar multiplication and is therefore not a valid vector space on its own.

blocks.text: Now try adding two whole-number vectors together instead of scaling, and notice that addition alone actually does preserve the whole-number property, showing that a set can satisfy one closure rule while still failing the other.
Key Takeaway

The neural network framing from section 11 is worth keeping in mind while reading model architecture diagrams, every dimension count quoted for a layer is quietly naming the size of a vector space, not just a number chosen for performance reasons.

A vector space is a set of vectors, of any kind, arrows, polynomials, matrices, or embeddings, that stays closed under addition and scalar multiplication, always satisfying a short list of predictable rules. Subspaces are smaller vector spaces obeying the same rules inside a larger one, and every embedding space used throughout AI is itself a genuine vector space in this formal sense.

This formal grounding is what justifies every piece of vector arithmetic covered elsewhere in this curriculum, addition, scaling, projection, and averaging all rely on the guarantee that the result always remains a valid, meaningful vector inside the same space it started in.

The high dimensional space and curse of dimensionality lessons immediately ahead in this module explore what happens as the dimension of a vector space grows very large, extending the foundation built here into genuinely counterintuitive territory.
